summary.title: Northstar cloud AI assistant
summary.description:
Assumptions: 

The current external LLM provider has an unspecified data retention policy
There are no limits on how many documents a customer can upload or how large documents can be
The audit log doesn't specify which staff member approved or denied a tool call
Staff approve tool calls inside the portal UI
MFA isn't enabled for staff sign-in

threats.title: B04: An attacker phishes a staff member's credentials and signs in as them
threats.description: If an attacker has access to a staff member's credentials then they can sign in (since no MFA is required) and fully access the data of the staff member's tenant. The attacker could also make incorrect approvals or cause additional harm to the tenant.
threats.mitigation: Introduce MFA, device attestation, and flag anomaly sign-in attempts within the identity provider (P1). With these controls in place, the number of breaches will decrease since there is an additional layer of security and successful breaches are more likely to be caught.

threats.title: B03: Approvals aren't linked to a specific staff member
threats.description: Staff members make the final decision on whether or not a tool call is accepted but there is no visibility into who accepted what, despite the presence of an audit log. If an incorrect approval or denial were to be made by a staff member, one couldn't trace the lineage back to them.
threats.mitigation: The staff members identifiers should be stored in the audit log (which we assume can't be altered) alongside the approval/denial verdict and additional information about the action that was committed. Now, each decision and output can be linked back to a staff member.

threats.title: B05: Many large documents get the Ingestion Worker stuck processing them
threats.description: Under the assumption that documents are processed sequentially in a queue, if many large documents are uploaded at the same time in the portal (P5) by an attacker, the ingestion worker could become delayed or stalled. The result of this is that the processing of documents uploaded by real customers might be delayed or dropped altogether.
threats.mitigation: Add file size and quantity limits in P5 and give the ingestion worker (P7) a predefined allocation of time to work on each document. Now, massive requests are ignored (and real users are told to chunk their uploads), and no document occupies too much valuable time on the processor (P7).

threats.title: B01: Malicious documents carry prompt-injection text
threats.description: If an attacker were to upload documents (P5) that contain hidden prompt injection instructions intended for an LLM, they would be treated exactly the same as documents uploaded by a real customer (i.e., they would be indexed and retrieved like any other document). Down the line this could lead to unintended behaviour by the LLM through malicious tool calls or inaccurate responses, among others.
threats.mitigation: The ingestion worker (P7) should label ALL uploaded documents as external (untrusted), and the assistant backend (P6) should structure the retrieved documents in a way that specifies that the documents cannot be treated as instructions. This way the severity and prevalence of prompt injection diminishes since hidden instructions are less likely to be executed.

threats.title: B02: Sensitive data is sent to the external LLM provider and potentially stored there
threats.description: Passing retrieved passages from P6 to P3 requires trust in the external LLM provider to not retain data and prompts. If the provider were to retain confidential data, and then they suffered a breach, the organization's data would be exposed.
threats.mitigation: Require a no-retention policy from the LLM provider (P3). Now, even if a breach were to occur to the external provider, there is no stored tenant data that can be exposed.
